depth: The depth map clearly represents the doorway scene’s 3D arrangement: the right doorframe wall is extremely close to the camera wearer (brightest white, ~0.3–0.5 m), the dog and wearer’s hands occupy the lower-left foreground (~0.4–1.2 m), the doorway partition wall sits behind the dog (~1.5 m), and the recessed storage space and left hallway extend into darkness (2–3+ m). In the foreground, the brightness gradient differentiates the wearer’s left hand (~0.4–0.5 m, holding the dog’s neck) and right hand (reaching toward the snout at ~0.5 m in frames 3–5) from the dog’s nearer head (~0.5–0.7 m, facing forward-right and tilting slightly upward in frame 3) and more distant hindquarters (~1.0–1.2 m on the left). Unlike the dark fur seen in the RGB frames, the depth map makes both the separation between the dog’s head and rear torso and the continuous surfaces of the floor and walls immediately understandable. However, it is unreliable within the dark closet and left hallway, where furniture and storage bags (~2–3 m away) collapse into uniform black. It also blends the wearer’s touching hands smoothly with the contours of the dog’s neck and snout, producing no sharp depth boundaries between them.
segmentation: The instance-segmentation map separates a foreground silhouette in the lower-left (approximately 0.4–1.2 m from the camera wearer and within arm’s reach) from an unsegmented black background, outlining together the dog standing from left to right and the wearer’s hands entering through the bottom edge. Across all five frames, the segmented foreground shows the dog raising its head slightly in frame 3 and turning its snout toward the wearer’s right hand at the bottom-center in frames 4–5, with the dog’s rear remaining on the left. Although the masks help distinguish the dark-furred dog from the shadowed floor and doorway corner in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5, both their class labels and boundary separation are highly unreliable. The system labels the dog and connected hands as a 'person' in frame 1, as overlapping 'cat'/'dog' regions in frame 2, and again as a 'person' in frame 3. In that third frame, it entirely cuts off the dog’s left-side hindquarters and incorrectly identifies a vertical laundry bag in the background closet (~2 m away) as another 'person'. Additionally, the wearer’s hands merge with the animal mask in frames 1–3, disappear completely in frame 4, and become fragmented purple masks with the lower chest beneath the green 'dog' mask in frame 5. Every wall, doorframe, and background object remains unsegmented.
pose: The pose map tries to assign yellow body keypoints to the lower-left foreground (~0.5–1.2 m away), where the dog stands within arm’s reach and the camera wearer’s hands extend upward from the frame’s bottom. Since the scene contains no complete human body—only the wearer’s two hands at ~0.4–0.5 m and the dog facing right with its head turned toward those hands—the map yields no dependable skeletal structure. Instead, it generates false-positive human torso/limb skeletons across the dog’s body in frames 1–3 and entirely blank results in frames 4–5. More precisely, the yellow body lines in frames 1 and 2 incorrectly stretch from the dog’s back on the left to its head on the right, then downward along the wearer’s left forearm. In frame 3, as the dog lifts its head toward the wearer, the skeleton contracts into a small cluster over the dog’s dark face. The map never detects magenta hand skeletons for either the wearer’s left hand, which holds the dog’s neck throughout all five frames, or the right hand, which points and reaches inward from the lower right in frames 1–5. Consequently, it supplies no useful spatial information beyond approximately indicating the dog’s foreground position during the first three frames.
